messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Elena Fischer is a 40-year-old data scientist who came to treatment after months of telling herself she should be able to think her way out of what had happened. Last year, while traveling in Israel for a work collaboration, she was on a bus that passed near an Arab village just after an outbreak of violence. She did not suffer a physical injury, but she watched another vehicle ahead erupt into flames after an attack. What stayed with her most was the suddenness of the fire, the shouting, and the helpless conviction that she was watching people trapped while she sat frozen, unable to do anything useful. Since then, she has carried a hard, punishing belief that she should have protected others and failed, and that a more capable person would never have ended up in that situation at all.

In the weeks after she returned home, the world became organized around reminders she had not expected. News footage, a restaurant conversation about the Middle East, or even driving past neighborhoods that somehow evoked the same dry, tense atmosphere as the villages she had seen could pull her up short. Fire was worst: a grill flare-up on a neighbor’s patio, candles, the orange reflection from a gas stove. At those moments she did not simply remember; the whole scene seemed to arrive without warning, more vivid than ordinary memory, with the sounds of shouting and the rush of the blaze in her head as if it were happening again. Those reminders also brought back her self-accusations with full force. Seeing flames or hearing someone mention Arab villages would make her think immediately, I failed them, somebody else would have acted, and on her darkest nights that would tip into the thought that maybe her own life was no longer worth much anyway.

As those memories took hold, Elena began reacting to the present as though danger were still close by. When a stranger approached too quickly in a parking lot or on the train platform, her body jolted and her mind leapt to threat before she could reason herself down. Living at that pitch of alertness, she found the world had become dense with reminders she could not stop reading: an idling bus, raised voices on the street, even the orange flare of a stove burner seemed to stand out immediately as possible signs that something was about to happen. During bad episodes she felt briefly as if she were back there, acting on pure alarm rather than awareness of where she really was. At home she started checking doors and windows repeatedly before bed, then again after getting into bed, because the sense of exposure would not settle. Stress made all of this worse; on pressured workdays, when deadlines stacked up or meetings ran long, she was more likely to startle, more likely to feel that a passing stranger might mean harm, and more likely to have the old scene burst back in uninvited.

Elena’s answer has been to stay mentally occupied at all costs. As a data scientist working mostly from home, she can disappear into code, model tuning, and late-night analyses for hours, and she has increasingly used that as a shield. When a news item, a flicker of flame, or a stressful day stirs the memories, she throws herself into work so she does not have to be alone with her thoughts. The same happens after nights of checking locks or after a flash of fear around a stranger; she opens her laptop and keeps going, telling herself productivity is the only thing keeping her together. Yet the overworking has narrowed her life. Her husband sees her staying at her desk long after dinner, not because the tasks are urgent but because stillness is dangerous.

The work does not quiet her mind as much as she hopes. While she is buried in spreadsheets or code, she finds herself circling the same question—why did this happen, why was she there, why didn’t she do more. That rumination keeps the event close and concrete, and the more she goes over it, the more readily the memory returns in full sensory form, complete with the sounds she heard that day. She has also noticed that after long stretches of overwork and isolation, she becomes less tolerant of stress and more vigilant in ordinary settings, and even small reminders in her environment become charged. In this way the strategies she relies on to escape the memories seem to leave her more vulnerable to the next surge of them, and more sensitive to flames, to geopolitical conversation, and to the tense associations that have attached themselves to Arab villages in her mind.

Over the past few months the loop has tightened. A memory arrives without warning, vivid and auditory, and she feels again that she failed. That conviction sharpens the memory further, as if self-reproach itself were a way of keeping the scene alive so she cannot ever excuse herself. She works later, checks the locks again, scans strangers more carefully, and becomes more stress-reactive, which only broadens the field of things that can set her off the next day. She finally sought help after her husband found her standing at the front door near midnight, checking it for the fourth time while a small fire pit from a neighbor’s yard flickered through the window. Elena told him she was exhausted and ashamed, and that what frightened her most was not only the memories themselves but the possibility that this was proof she was as weak and culpable as she already believed. What she hopes for, cautiously, is some way to be in her own life again without every stressor, every stranger, and every flash of flame turning the past into the present.

violation_explanations: The vignette does not clearly state in the same paragraph that Elena’s sense of threat or danger directly leads to reminders/cues becoming triggers, despite describing both threat and many reminders.
